source_text: Sed quid nos ad parvulos; cum quaestio Manichaeorum nec perfectae aetatis hominem dicat voluntate peccare? Nam si ideo exortum est in homine malum, quia de nihilo factus erat, a necessario autem habuit homo ut de nihilo fieret; sine dubio malum non a possibili, sed a necessario recepit. Quod quia longa disputatione destructum est, adhuc modicum, quo magis ac magis iteratione lucescat, super hoc eodem disseramus. Quaeris ergo unde ipsa voluntas mala in primo homine exstiterit. Respondeo: De motu animi, cogente nullo. Quaeris et unde ipse motus. Respondeo: Quid requiris? Unde esse potuerit, an unde esse compulsus sit? Si dicas, quod scripsisti quoque: Unde esse compulsus est, referam te asystata et contraria loqui. Quaeris enim quis coegerit, quod esse non possit, nisi cogente nullo; quod quia ipsa sui contrarietate dissolvitur, nihil habet virium quaestio, quae ordinem non habet. Igitur stolidissime interrogas, unde ipsa voluntas mala. Hoc enim quod dicis: Unde, non occasionem, sed originem eius, id est, naturam requiris; at id, sicut supra tractatum est, si naturam accipit, definitionem sui perdit, qua dictum est: cogente nullo; si vero definitionem tenet, praeiudicium nativitatis excludit. Non ideo ergo peccavit homo, quia de nihilo factus est, non ideo quia a Deo factus est, non ideo quia de tenebris factus est, non ideo quia liberi arbitrii factus est; sed ideo peccavit, quia voluit; id est, ideo habuit voluntatem malam, quia voluit.
pass_a_gloss: But what is this to us toward little ones; when the question of the Manichaeans says not even a human of perfect age sins by will? For if therefore evil arose in the human, because he had been made from nothing, but the human had from the necessary that he be made from nothing; without doubt he received evil not from the possible, but from the necessary. Which because it has been destroyed by a long disputation, still a little, that more and more it may shine by iteration, let us discuss upon this same. You ask therefore from where the evil will itself existed in the first human. I reply: From a motion of the mind, no one compelling. You ask also from where the motion itself. I reply: What do you seek? From where it could be, or from where it was compelled to be? If you say, what you also wrote: From where it was compelled to be, I will report that you speak unsystematic and contrary things. For you ask who compelled that which cannot be except with no one compelling; which because it is dissolved by its own contrariety, the question which does not have order has no powers. Most stolidly therefore you interrogate, from where the evil will itself. For this which you say: From where, you seek not its occasion but its origin, that is nature; but that, as was treated above, if it receives a nature, loses the definition of itself, by which it was said: no one compelling; but if it holds the definition, it excludes a prior judgment of nativity. Not therefore therefore did the human sin, because he was made from nothing, not therefore because he was made by God, not therefore because he was made from darkness, not therefore because he was made of free decision; but therefore he sinned, because he willed; that is, therefore he had an evil will, because he willed.

pass_b_english: But why turn to infants, when the Manichaeans’ question does not allow even an adult to sin by will? If evil arose in a human being because he was made from nothing, and he necessarily received his making from nothing, he undoubtedly received evil from necessity, not possibility. Although lengthy argument has destroyed this, let us discuss the same point a little longer, so that repetition makes it increasingly clear. You ask where the evil will itself existed in the first man. I answer: from a movement of the mind under no compulsion. You ask where that movement itself came from. I answer: what are you asking? Where it could come from, or from what it was compelled to exist? If you say, as you also wrote, ‘From what it was compelled to exist,’ I reply that your words are inconsistent and contradictory. You ask who compelled something that cannot exist except under no compulsion. This dissolves through its own contradiction; a question without order has no force.

You therefore ask with great foolishness where the evil will itself comes from. By ‘where,’ you ask not its occasion but its origin, that is, its nature. Yet, as discussed above, if it receives a nature, it loses its own definition, which says ‘under no compulsion’; if it retains its definition, it excludes predetermination by birth. The human being therefore sinned not because he was made from nothing, not because he was made by God, not because he was made from darkness, and not because he was made with free will. He sinned because he willed: that is, he had an evil will because he willed.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
